part_title: Managed AI APIs and Amazon Comprehend Text Analysis
review_basis: Original AIF Module 08 numbered WebPs visually inspected one by one on 2026-11-14; rewritten concise visual-first narration based on actual diagram order, figures, examples and visible caveats; fresh audio required.

scenes.title: Why AWS AI Managed Services?
scenes.narration: Start with the top row: this slide matches a business input to a purpose-built AWS service. Text goes to Comprehend for language, key phrases and sentiment, or Translate for another language. Recorded speech goes to Transcribe to become text; Polly works the other way, converting text into spoken audio. For images, Rekognition examines visual content, whereas Textract reads scanned documents and extracts fields. A chatbot needing conversation intent points to Lex; product recommendations to Personalize; enterprise search is illustrated with Kendra. Now look below. A frustrated password-reset email enters Comprehend. The sample result identifies negative sentiment, key phrases and English. Beside it, Textract reads an invoice and returns number INV-1001, vendor ACME Ltd and the illustrated total of 1,250 dollars. Both are managed APIs for a known task. The green panel contrasts this with SageMaker AI, which is appropriate when you need to build and train a custom model. The deciding question is not simply 'is this AI?' but 'what input and output do I need?'

scenes.title: Amazon Comprehend
scenes.narration: Follow the top flow from left to right. The email says, 'Delivery to Chennai was late, but support helped.' Amazon Comprehend processes the plain text using natural language processing, meaning software that identifies useful patterns in human language. The results panel illustrates detected language English, the location entity Chennai, phrases delivery and support, and mixed sentiment. That makes sense: the delivery was bad but the support was helpful. The CRM dashboard then lets an analyst prioritize the issue without losing context. The lower-left panel repeats the same example, rather than describing another workflow. In the middle, topic modeling groups many emails into themes such as refunds and delivery issues; that pictured capability is historical and should not be assumed available to new customers. Finally compare the bottom-right cards. Comprehend analyzes text that you already have. Textract first reads scanned documents and their layout. For a scanned invoice, extract with Textract before any optional language analysis with Comprehend. These result boxes are illustrative, not exact API JSON.

scenes.title: Comprehend – Custom Classification
scenes.narration: This slide distinguishes custom classification from ready-made text analysis. Follow the five numbered boxes. First, people label support messages as billing or delivery and store training data in Amazon S3. Second, Amazon Comprehend trains a custom classifier to recognize these organization-specific categories. Third, a new message arrives: 'I was charged twice for my order. Can you help me?' Fourth, the classifier predicts the label billing. Fifth, the application routes the ticket to the Billing team. The lower-left example shows the same decision path in more detail. Notice the separation of responsibility: Comprehend predicts a category; your application implements ticket routing. On the lower right, the ready-made APIs identify general sentiment or common entities without your own labels. A custom classifier requires labeled examples but can learn your particular categories, such as technical support. Evaluate its predictions on separate test messages because labels can be wrong. If the task asks which team should receive a message, choose classification, not entity recognition.

scenes.title: Named Entity Recognition (NER)
scenes.narration: Look at the highlighted words in the sentence: 'Maya met the team in Seattle on Tuesday.' Amazon Comprehend identifies Maya as a PERSON, Seattle as a LOCATION and Tuesday as a DATE. This is named entity recognition, often shortened to NER. It finds spans of text and assigns entity types; it does not summarize the whole sentence or decide its sentiment. The top arrows show input text, analysis, then extracted entities. Now compare the two lower panels. Standard recognition handles common types such as person, location and date. On the right, 'The policy ACME-12345 was updated' contains a business-specific policy ID. A custom entity recognizer can be trained to extract ACME-12345 as POLICY_ID when standard categories do not cover it. This is different from custom classification: entity recognition finds a particular phrase inside the text, while classification assigns a label to the entire document. Choose according to the information the business needs.

scenes.title: Comprehend – Custom Entity Recognition
scenes.narration: The top architecture shows how a company teaches Comprehend a new entity type. Start with labeled policy documents stored in Amazon S3; examples identify text spans as POLICY_ID. Comprehend trains a custom entity recognizer from these annotations. A customer then writes, 'Please review policy PL-2048.' The trained recognizer finds the actual text PL-2048 and returns it as an entity with type POLICY_ID. The claims application can use that value to look up a policy; Comprehend itself does not decide whether a claim is valid. The lower-left worked example displays a sample policy document, the incoming message and the extracted value, in that order. In the middle, standard NER finds general people, places and dates; custom recognition finds terms you define for your organization. The right panel compares processing modes: real-time analysis returns results for a single text request, while asynchronous processing handles batches of documents from S3. Both need quality checks using representative documents to detect missed or incorrect policy numbers.
